scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a qualified position that the welfare of the people is the surest sign of greatness while achievements still matter; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Nations are often remembered for their famous leaders, artists, and scientists.
Some people argue that the surest sign of a great nation is not these achievements but the general welfare of its ordinary people.
I largely agree that the welfare of the people is the best measure of greatness, though remarkable achievements still matter as part of the picture.

sections.role: Body 1 — Welfare as the clearest measure

sentences.text: First, the well-being of ordinary people is the clearest test of how well a nation actually works.
A country may produce brilliant art or science while most of its citizens remain poor, sick, or unfree.
For example, a nation with grand monuments but hungry children has clearly failed at its most basic duty.
This shows that achievements mean little if the people who make up the nation do not live decent lives.
Widespread health, education, and security affect everyone, not just a gifted few.
Any government that cares for all its citizens has met the deepest purpose of a nation.
By this measure, general welfare is rightly seen as the surest indicator of greatness.
Second, however, the achievements of rulers, artists, and scientists should not be dismissed entirely.
Great discoveries and works of art often improve the welfare of the people themselves.
Consider the way medical research extends ordinary lives, or how great literature shapes a society's values.
Such achievements are not separate from welfare but are often one of its causes.
Societies that value learning and creativity usually become healthier and wealthier as a result.
These accomplishments can also give a people pride and a shared sense of identity.
In this way, achievement and welfare support each other rather than standing apart.
In conclusion, the general welfare of the people is the truest measure of a great nation.
But the achievements of its thinkers and artists matter too, because they often raise that welfare and enrich its meaning.
Greatness, in the end, belongs to the nation that turns its talents toward the good of all its people.
